title: Decision Documentation
description: Learn how to document technical decisions effectively using ADRs, RFCs, and decision logs so teams can understand context and avoid repeating past debates.

data.text: Every technical decision has context. Why did we choose this database? Why did we reject that framework? Six months later, the people who made the decision may have left, and the team is left wondering whether the choice still makes sense. Decision documentation preserves that context.

Good decision documentation is not about bureaucracy. It is about reducing future confusion, preventing re-litigation of settled debates, and helping new team members understand the system quickly. The best documentation is brief, honest, and easy to find.

An Architecture Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that captures a single decision. ADRs are lightweight by design — usually one or two pages — so they are easy to write and easy to read. The format was popularized by Michael Nygard and has become a standard practice in many engineering organizations.

data.content: A standard template for architecture decision records.
data.code:
# ADR 12: Use PostgreSQL for User Data

## Status
Accepted

## Context
We need a database for user profiles, preferences, and authentication data.
The team has experience with PostgreSQL and MySQL. We expect 100K to 500K
users in the first year.

## Decision
We will use PostgreSQL for all user-related data.

## Consequences
Positive:
- Team familiarity reduces implementation time
- Strong ACID guarantees protect user data
- Rich extension ecosystem (pgvector for future features)

Negative:
- Vertical scaling is more expensive than alternatives
- Requires careful connection pool management

## Alternatives Considered
- MySQL: Similar capabilities, less team experience
- MongoDB: More flexible schema, weaker consistency guarantees

## Related Decisions
- ADR 8: Use Redis for session storage

data.text: Not every decision deserves an ADR. Focus on decisions that are hard to reverse, expensive to change, or surprising to future engineers. Good candidates include: choosing a core technology, adopting a new pattern, defining an API contract, or deciding how to handle cross-cutting concerns like authentication or logging.

items: Technology choices: databases, frameworks, cloud services
Architecture patterns: microservices, event sourcing, CQRS
API design: REST conventions, versioning strategy, authentication
Data models: schema design, partitioning strategy, consistency model
Operational choices: deployment strategy, monitoring approach, incident response

data.text: ADRs should be short enough that people actually read them. One to two pages is ideal. Use clear headings, bullet points instead of paragraphs when possible, and include a decision date. Store ADRs in a dedicated docs/decisions folder in the repository so they are versioned alongside the code they describe.

data.content: A concise ADR for a real decision.
data.code:
# ADR 23: Use TypeScript Strict Mode

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2025-03-15

## Context
Our codebase has accumulated implicit any types and unchecked nulls.
Bugs from these issues have increased 30 percent in the last quarter.

## Decision
Enable TypeScript strict mode across all packages.

## Consequences
- Existing code needs type fixes (estimated 2 sprints)
- Fewer runtime type errors after migration
- Better IDE support and autocomplete

## Alternatives
- Enable strict mode gradually per-package (slower, more complex)
- Add runtime type checks instead (does not catch all issues)

data.text: ADRs are great for point-in-time decisions, but teams also need a running record of ongoing debates and context. A decision log is a lighter-weight alternative — a single document that tracks the current thinking on open questions, assumptions being tested, and decisions pending review. Update it as context changes.

A decision that is documented but impossible to find is useless. Store ADRs in a dedicated folder in the repository. Use a consistent naming convention like ADR-001-title.md. Add an index file that links to all ADRs and includes a one-line summary of each. Link to ADRs from the code they affect using code comments when relevant.

data.title: Make It Easy to Add Decisions
data.text: If creating an ADR requires five meetings and a template approval process, people will skip it. The process should take 30 minutes. Start with a template, fill in the essentials, and refine the format as your team learns what works.

terms.definition: A short document capturing a single architectural decision, its context, and its consequences.
A running document tracking open questions, assumptions, and ongoing technical decisions.
The implied cost of future rework caused by choosing a quick or easy solution today.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Document decisions that are hard to reverse or expensive to change
Use ADRs for point-in-time decisions, decision logs for ongoing context
Keep ADRs brief: one to two pages, not a novel
Store decisions in a dedicated, versioned folder in the repository
Include context, alternatives, consequences, and the decision date
Make it easy to add decisions, or people will not do it
data.takeaway: Decision documentation turns invisible institutional knowledge into a durable resource that helps teams move faster with confidence.
